edition.locus: Eusebius HE 5.1.20-23 (Sanctus unbent; the heavenly water)

source_text: Ὁ δὲ Σάγκτος καὶ αὐτὸς ὑπερβεβλημένως καὶ ὑπὲρ πάντα ἄνθρωπον πάσας τὰς ἐξ ἀνθρώπων αἰκίας γενναίως ὑπομένων, τῶν ἀνόμων ἐλπιζόντων διὰ τὴν ἐπιμονὴν καὶ τὸ μέγεθος τῶν βασάνων ἀκούσεσθαί τι παρ᾽ αὐτοῦ τῶν μὴ δεόντων, τοσαύτῃ ὑποστάσει ἀντιπαρετάξατο αὐτοῖς, ὥστε μηδὲ ἴδιον κατεῖπεν ὄνομα μήτε ἔθνους μήτε πόλεως ὅθεν ἦν, μηδὲ εἰ δοῦλος ἢ ἐλεύθερος εἴη· ἀλλὰ πρὸς πάντα τὰ ἐπερωτώμενα ἀπεκρίνατο τῇ Ῥωμαϊκῇ φωνῇ· Χριστιανός εἰμι. Τοῦτο καὶ ἀντὶ ὀνόματος καὶ ἀντὶ πόλεως καὶ ἀντὶ γένους καὶ ἀντὶ παντὸς ἐπαλλήλως ὡμολόγει, ἄλλην δὲ φωνὴν οὐκ ἤκουσαν αὐτοῦ τὰ ἔθνη. Ὅθεν δὴ καὶ φιλονεικία μεγάλη τοῦ τε ἡγεμόνος καὶ τῶν βασανιστῶν ἐγένετο πρὸς αὐτόν, ὥστε ὁπότε μηκέτι μηδὲν εἶχον ὃ ποιήσωσιν αὐτῷ, τὸ τελευταῖον χαλκᾶς λεπίδας διαπύρους προσεκόλλων τοῖς τρυφερωτάτοις μέλεσι τοῦ σώματος αὐτοῦ. Καὶ ταῦτα μὲν ἐκαίετο, αὐτὸς δὲ παρέμενεν ἀνεπίκαμπτος καὶ ἀνένδοτος, στερεὸς πρὸς τὴν ὁμολογίαν, ὑπὸ τῆς οὐρανίου πηγῆς τοῦ ὕδατος τῆς ζωῆς τοῦ ἐξιόντος ἐκ τῆς νηδύος τοῦ Χριστοῦ δροσιζόμενος καὶ ἐνδυναμούμενος· τὸ δὲ σωμάτιον μάρτυς ἦν τῶν συμβεβηκότων, ὅλον τραῦμα καὶ μώλωψ καὶ συνεσπασμένον καὶ ἀποβεβληκὸς τὴν ἀνθρώπειον ἔξωθεν μορφήν, ἐν ᾧ πάσχων Χριστὸς μεγάλας ἐπετέλει δόξας, καταργῶν τὸν ἀντικείμενον καὶ εἰς τὴν τῶν λοιπῶν ὑποτύπωσιν ὑποδεικνύων ὅτι μηδὲν φοβερὸν ὅπου πατρὸς ἀγάπη, μηδὲ ἀλγεινὸν ὅπου Χριστοῦ δόξα.
pass_a_gloss: But Sanctus himself also, nobly enduring beyond measure and beyond every man all the torments from men, when the lawless hoped that through persistence and the greatness of the tortures they would hear something improper from him, opposed them with such firm resistance that he declared neither his own name nor nation nor city from which he was, nor whether he was slave or free; but to all the questions he answered in the Latin tongue: I am a Christian. This he confessed repeatedly instead of name and instead of city and instead of race and instead of everything, and the nations heard no other voice from him. Whence a great contention of the governor and the torturers arose against him, so that when they no longer had anything that they might do to him, at last they applied red-hot bronze plates to the most tender members of his body. And those members were being burned, but he remained unbending and unyielding, solid toward the confession, being cooled and strengthened by the heavenly spring of the water of life coming out of the belly of Christ; and the little body was a witness of what had happened, wholly wound and bruise and drawn together and having lost the outward human form, in which suffering Christ accomplished great glories, annulling the Adversary and showing for the pattern of the rest that nothing is fearful where the Father's love is, nor painful where Christ's glory is.
pass_b_english: But Sanctus himself also endured nobly every torment men devised, beyond measure and beyond what any man could bear. The lawless men hoped that his long endurance and the severity of his tortures would at last force some forbidden word from him, yet he set such steadfast resolve against them that he would not declare his own name, nor his people, nor the city he came from, nor whether he was slave or free. To every question put to him he answered in Latin, I am a Christian. That confession he repeated again and again instead of name, instead of city, instead of race, instead of everything else, and the pagans heard no other utterance from him.

A fierce contest of wills therefore arose between him and the governor and his torturers, until, when they had nothing left to do to him, they finally pressed red-hot plates of bronze against the tenderest parts of his body. His flesh burned, but he remained unbending and unyielding, firm in his confession, cooled and strengthened by the heavenly spring of the water of life flowing from the belly of Christ (cf. John 7:38). His poor body bore witness to what had been done, for it was all wound and bruise, contracted and stripped of its outward human shape. Yet in that suffering body the suffering Christ accomplished great triumphs, stripping the Adversary of power and showing, as a pattern for the rest, that nothing is fearful where the Father's love is present, and nothing is painful where Christ's glory is present.

lemmas.gloss: drew himself up in opposition against

choices.why: φωνῇ here means language, and Ῥωμαϊκῇ in this judicial context denotes Latin rather than Greek
dative of means with ἀντιπαρετάξατο describes the manner of resistance, not metaphysical substance
in context it denotes the persecuting outsiders listening for another answer, not nations in general
